title: Services and the journal
subtitle: systemd is the operating system’s control plane. Learn to ask it what is true.
objectives: Explain units, targets, and the difference between active and enabled
Start, stop, restart, enable, and mask services
Read service state and logs with systemctl and journalctl
Find failed units and investigate this boot
Understand when a daemon-reload is required

lab.title: Investigate a service like an operator
lab.scenario: Answer the four questions: is it running, will it start at boot, what does it say, and what else failed?

steps.text: Inspect SSH state and boot posture.
steps.cmd: systemctl status sshd && systemctl is-enabled sshd

steps.text: Read the last 20 journal lines for SSH.
steps.verify: The journal should show sshd startup or connection entries with no permission errors.

steps.text: List every failed unit on the system.
steps.verify: An empty list is a valid and useful result.

steps.text: Show the default boot target and running services.
steps.verify: get-default should print a target such as multi-user.target, and running services should be listed.

steps.text: Install a service package, enable it, verify it, then disable it.
steps.cmd: sudo dnf install -y httpd && sudo systemctl enable --now httpd && systemctl is-active httpd && sudo systemctl disable --now httpd
steps.verify: is-active should print active after enable --now, then inactive after disable --now.

quiz.q: What is the difference between active and enabled?
options: Active means running now; enabled means starts at boot
Enabled means running now; active means installed
quiz.why: A service can be running without being enabled, or enabled but currently stopped or failed.

quiz.q: Which command shows logs for a single systemd unit?
quiz.why: journalctl -u filters the journal by unit. Add --since, -f, or -p for more control.

quiz.q: When must you run systemctl daemon-reload?
quiz.why: systemd caches unit definitions. daemon-reload makes it re-read unit files from disk.
